prerequisites: Basic knowledge of materials science (Fe-C diagram, hardness,...)
Basic knowledge of mechanics (forces, powers, drives,...)

learning_outcomes.text: Provide insight into the functioning and organization of discrete-goods manufacturing companies and their various departments: engineering, work preparation, production, quality control, etc.

Familiarize the student with the basic concepts and theories of production processes: specifically, machining processes (e.g., milling or grinding), forming processes (e.g., sheet bending, punching), welding processes, etc.

Impart the basic knowledge necessary for further study on flexible production systems, automation and mechatronics in production, computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing), mechanical machining, forming (forging, extrusion, injection molding,...), non-conventional machining (laser beam, water jet, electrochemical machining, stereolithography,...), etc.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to discrete production:

Functioning of a discrete-goods manufacturing company; division of tasks among departments; relationship design-production, production-work preparation, production-quality assurance, production-production planning, etc.

Overview of production processes: primary forming (e.g., casting), forming (e.g., forging), machining (e.g., milling), non-conventional machining (e.g., laser machining), material growth techniques (rapid prototyping), joining (e.g., welding), post-treatment (e.g., hardening or coating).
Basic concepts of machining: tools, tool geometry, machining parameters (cutting speed, feed, engagement), cut, chip slenderness, etc.
Materials for cutting tools for machining and forming.
Basic theory of machining illustrated with an example of a single-point cutting technique, in this case 'turning':
Physical models
Empirical models: tool life equation, cutting force equation,...
Cost calculation, optimization and introduction to work preparation.
Example of a machining technique with multiple controlled cutting edges, in this case 'milling':
Description and concepts;
Application/extension of theory.
Example of a machining technique with multiple uncontrolled cutting edges, in this case 'grinding':
Description and concepts;
Application/extension of theory.
Example of a forming technique, in this case 'sheet metal working by punching, bending and cutting':
Description and concepts;
Application and theory.
Example of a joining technique, in this case 'welding'.
Seminars and practicals: A total of eight assignments where the student produces products in the workshop on manually operated machines and on computer-controlled machines (CNC).
Demonstrations on both conventional and non-conventional production machines (including laser cutting, spark erosion, stereolithography, robots).
Other topics introduced during film sessions and computer exercises.
assessment_rules: The evaluation of seminars and practicals is incorporated into the exam points for the entire course. The assessment consists of a written exam with an oral explanation. Question types include multiple-choice, open, and closed questions. Students may use a formularium and calculator during the exam.
